The Lambda of Psi Upsilon Keeps
Pace With the Lion of Columbia
By Richard R. Szathmary, Lambda '67
Lambda Chapter
1842
In 1842, when a few presumably be
whiskered young gentleman blades of
New York society gathered to form the
Lambda Chapter of Psi Upsilon, Co
lumbia University was a
vastly different
place than today. Its location at 49th and
Madison, modern midtown, was a semirural backwater of depressing Gothicstyle halls much like many of Yale's build
ings remain today, and the pace of life at
the Lambda, its energizing atmosphere if
you will, was
surely as slow and every bit
as genteel as Columbia's own physical
surroundings in what then constituted a
sleepy residential precinct of upper Man
hattan. Columbia University's mascot,
the lion, rarely roared but, instead, gent
ly purred.
Today, of course, Columbia and the
Lambda are both much farther uptown,
in a no longer pokey area where all-night
delis and Korean-owned fruit and vege
table stands and somewhat tawdry neigh
borhood bars and Cuban-Chinese res
taurants exist cheek by jowl with impos
ing academic edifices and staid professo
rial residences. But it's even more
impor
tant now to keep that idea of pacing in
mind when considering the Lambda, this
year's honored host of the 139th annual
Convention, and its environs. Columbia,
in short, is an urban as weU as a tradi
tionally urbane university, and the role
into which that forces fraternity life at
Columbia makes the Lambda in certain
respects almost utterly unlike any other
Psi U Chapters save the Delta and Ome
ga. Fratemity life in such an area faces
somewhat different challenges, offers
somewhat additional benefits. And all,
perhaps, at a
vastly different level of in
tensity and feeling than experienced at
other colleges and universities.
Each and every Chapter, after all,
could proudly proclaim (often to unduly
immodest length) its alumni accomplish
ments, the key role it's played on campus,
the architectural glories of its Chapter
House, the fiercely felt joys ofits brother
hood over the years, even its mildly ris
que reputation for hard partying.
None of this persiflage, however, de
fines the essence of a Chapter, really ex
plains what makes up its internal dy
namics or its special relationship to and
within Psi Upsilon.
But it's a htde different for the Lamb
da. A crucial little, whereby pace has be
come transmuted into tradition, even as
tradition has helped define pace. And
there are five key figures who should be
looked at more closely for the sort of requisitely better understanding of what the
Lambda is and how it works.
In 1882, Nicholas Murray Butler was a
Lambda brother and graduating Co
lumbia senior at a
university whose presi
dent was then Frederick Barnard, after
whom Barnard College was
eventually
named. By then, too, Columbia was firm
ly ensconced in its present location upon
the former Revolutionary War battlefield
of Morningside Heights. The prevailing
atmosphere was of gentility and
quietude. Both Henry James and Edith
Wharton, alive and well then, would have
felt eminently comfortable amid such sur
roundings, where gentlemen stiU wore
frock coats and called for their young
ladies in carriages.
Yet Nicholas Murray Butler was a
very
different fish than even his Fraternity
brothers, let alone the rest of his graduat
ing class, and he wound up showing them
all something about pace and drive by the
ease with which, upon his entering
academe rather than business like almost
everyone else, he sped through advanced
study in Europe and his ensuing Co
lumbia career. By 1902, in fact, just twen
ty years after graduation, Buder was
named president of Columbia, a post he
wound up hanging on to until 1945.
And as
University prexy, Butler surely
imparted much of his renowned personal
energy to his beloved Fraternity Chap
ter. The University added school after
school, new division after division; the
Lambda became stronger and better re
garded on
campus.
There was no lazy basking in Butler's
reflected glory, ofcourse
(though it plain
ly never hurts to have a brother so
highly
placed), but there was
certainly a glorious
model right on
campus for the Chapter to
look up to and learn from, a
privilege that
was granted to several generations of
Lambdas during Butler's long presiden
tial tenure. Mammoth Butler Library,
where the book-stuffed stacks literally
seem long and wide enough to serve as
landing ramps for carrier-based jets, is
but one concrete dollop of testimony to
this particular Lambda's strong impact on
Columbia.
The examples set by Nicholas Murray
Butler, incidentally, cannot but have
deeply impressed a Lambda of the Class
of 1903 who'd seen Butler's accession to
the University presidency first-hand,
named MarceUus Hartley Dodge.
Heir to the Remington Arms fortune
and an avid varsity athlete. Dodge was
also someone who, when he saw some
thing on
campus that could be aided by
his talents and/or background, was happy
to use his full family wherewithal to get
the job done.
Disappointed at the lack of acceptable
dorm rooms during his fi-eshman year
(this story is Columbia history cannily
transmogrified into Psi U folklore).
Dodge petitioned his doting mother to
provide more suitable accommodations
for his student brethren �
hence Hartley
Hall, where many Convention delegates
will be staying.
During his entire career, Dodge
showed great generosity toward both his
Fratemity and his alma mater, and in so
doing set a
dizzying pace of gift-giving
that coUege officials everywhere probably

sorely wish they could see
duplicated in
just one or two alums a
generation, let
alone every few years. Marcellus Hartley
Dodge may not have set the definitive
tone for the Lambda Chapter through his
more than six decades of association with
the Chapter (he died in the '60s), of
course. Yet by sheer dint of his largesse
he remains a major influence upon the
Lambda. From more composed times
(which Mark Twain once called "the
Gilded Age") to the anguish and torment
that began hitting the Columbia campus
in the early '60s, his sense of fraternal
brotherhood and devotion to his alma ma
ter never faltered.
Another Lambda lucky enough to per
sonally view President Butler in action
came out of the Class of 1924, the period
of bathtub gin, flappers, the Charleston
and flagpole sitting, which pulp writers
and even good ones like John O'Hara and
F. Scott Fitzgerald have incessantly char
acterized as prime time for fraternitystyle nonsense, for collegiate partying
and the clich6d carefree approach to both
studies and life in general.
But even ifthe goings on from that time
set an incorrect, deleterious image to
fratemity Ufe for several decades after
ward, unfortunately, it wasn't that way for
Ferris Willis Booth, Class of '24. By all
accounts, both as an undergrad and
graduate, he was extremely hard-working
and dedicated.
And, keeping up the pace of involve
ment previously set by Butler and
Dodge, Ferris Booth became a major
donor to the University. Perhaps just as
you're reading this, delegates to the Con
vention are meeting in the building he
donated, that's named after him, Ferris
Booth Hall. That makes three buildings
named after distinguished Lambdas on
what, compared to most non-urban
schools, is a small, compact campus;
that's not a bad record, either.
Incidentally, a
distinguished sculptor
made what we like to think of as a Psi U
contribution to Columbia's campus
architecture. The famous statue oi Alma
Mater that dominates Low Plaza, sculpt
ed by Daniel Chester French, conceals
an owl, rather craftily, in the folds of the
statue's robe. Knowing Lambdas have
delighted for many years in pointing this
out to friends and relatives as a bit of
fraternal arcana.
After Ferris Booth's time, however,
the Lambda finally fell full prey to the
curious dilemmas urban universities pose
for fraternities.
Previously, during the times of Butler,
Dodge and Booth, New York City was
still a more relaxed, smaller-scale social
venue, particularly up on Morningside
Heights, where fraternities did indeed
dominate what social life existed up
there.
Yet, as New York grew, so did the
varied enticements of "downtown," glit
tering prizes that to a great extent tem
porarily blocked out fratemity values and
ties. It was the old "How ya gonna keep
'em down on the farm ..." syndrome all
over again.
It wasn't a
rapid decUne for the Lamb
da, ofcourse �
it was more Uke a gradual
ly shrinking series of peaks and valleys
during which, nevertheless, the Chapter
graduated every bit as many scholars and
athletes and sent heroes off to war as aU
other Psi U chapters �
but, once past the
social somnolence of the post-World War
II '40s and '50s, the late '60s found die
Lambda Chapter in bad, almost pitifiil,
shape.
When students are
taking on the gov
ernment and protesting to "save" the
world or at least their country, for exam
ple, and have a city the size of New York
to do it in plus a
myriad of things to do and
see
off-campus after the protest rally, the
social attractions of Friday night beer taps
pale badly by comparison.
From such happenstances, too, arise
strong feelings, especially prevalent at an
already highly politicized school like Co
lumbia, that fratemities are inimical to
academic values and political "progress,"
coupled with resultant, sometimes over
whelming, peer pressure to avoid
fraternities like the proverbial plague.
These conditions during the '60s affected
all fraternities at Columbia, not just the
Lambda, and forced a palpable sense of
irrelevancy on the remaining brothers,
who often seemed to rate and treat them
selves as an ailing pack of dinosaurs much
given to self-piteous crying in their too
many beers.
At the Lambda in particular, however,
the constant interest and concern of Dick
Ross, Lambda '20, serving as president of
the Lambda Association, was always
there to remind the membership of their
responsibilities to themselves, each
other, and to Psi Upsilon. It wasn't easy,
but, without Brother Ross' often barkingly delivered administration, it would
have been totally impossible for the
Lambda to survive.
Clearly, then, the pace of the '70s and
its attendant problems demanded some
one with the drive of Nicholas Murray
Butler, but more forward looking than
that old gentleman (who, it is usually con
ceded, stayed too long at his presidential
post), as well as someone who could
emphasize to brothers and potential
pledges alike the attractions of a fraternal
unit even in a city like New York, who
could then emphasize why such units are
actually necessary to offset pressures
otherwise put on students by a cit> and
urban university's enforced anonymity.
In short, the Lambda needed a spokes
man who actually knew the considerable
case against fratemities at an urban uni
versity and understood it thoroughh , but
could answer back with replies that would
today or even back then also gratif. the
Ukes of Ferris Booth and Marcellus Hart
ley Dodge.
Luckily for the Lambda, that rare per
sonage was located in Murra\- Eskenazi,
Lambda '56. Coming into a situation
where alumni support had dropped off
precipitously, where the House was
down to three brothers and was occupied
by non-brothers, Murray Eskenazi, aided
by the Pamphratria, Columbia's version
of the Interfraternity Council, actually
went out and got the Chapter some out
standing pledges, in addition to all his
other efforts toward the Lambda's come
back.
He was
greatly assisted in this bird-dog
effort by Brother Robert Morey, Pi '20,
then President of the Executive Council,
who assured and guaranteed that the In
ternational Office was completely behind
him. A diadem, after all, is composed of
several jewels, and Psi Upsilon would
have shown far less bright without the
Lambda. So, with Brother Morey's ear
and assistance always there, Murray took
on a task that several contemporary
Lambda alumni had already, in fact, dis
missed as basically hopeless.
Nor have those prodigious, greatly
appreciated efforts of his ever even re
motely slackened off. Murray is every bit
as involved with the Lambda today as he's
been over the past ten years of recovery,
when he literally near-singlehandedly
pulled the host Chapter of this year's
Convention back from the edge of sheer
extinction.
So look carefully around you as you
visit the Lambda. Talk to the brothers,
male and female. See for yourself how
positive they sound, how large and wellorganized the Chapter is, how sincerely,
without even a faint trace of Falwellian
hokiness, its members speak of worthy
values that are otherwise in all too scant
evidence both on the Columbia campus
and in New York proper.
The resurgence of the Lambda, which
Murray Eskenazi was so
crucially in
strumental in, is a
living, large-scale
testament to the idea that fraternities
have a role in the urban university. The
Lambda, by virtue of the considerable
friendships, sense of dedication and
values it fosters, becomes absolutely
necessary in a fashion that brothers from
other schools uuu never ftill\ compre
hend. The Chapter survixos in tlic City

plement its general operating funds. The

endowment which will provide funds for

solid base from which we can operate and

for the future needs of our members.
Without the endowment we could not
provide the quality programs we have.

nificant ff it were not for our endowment.

ment is the most meaningfiil of all gifts.

strate how tax incentives may make it

As you consider a gfft, bear in mind the

plore new areas while being guided by
seasoned alumni. Alumni play the
most important role in the develop
ment of a man's career plans. They
